prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological classification of insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I have moved from B046 to B028 as my preferred single-part prize. The scientific case for B028 is a complete chain: Kane and Mele's 2005 papers introduced the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 invariant, which says that a band structure with time-reversal symmetry can be topologically nontrivial and must then carry protected edge or surface states. Molenkamp's group observed the predicted edge transport in HgTe quantum wells in 2007. From the electronic-structure side, this changed how we classify and search for materials, and fifteen to twenty years of independent confirmation by transport, ARPES, STM and imaging in many materials leave the interpretation stable. The round-1 exchange also removed the problem I weighted most in my own ranking, because Danielsson, Johansson, Olsson, Kroll and Lindroth all converged on Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the defensible trio, and Danielsson dropped his earlier preference for Hasan over Mele. That settles the three-name allocation in a way the B046 discussion did not settle its third slot.
statement.case_against: The credit is still incomplete. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's 2006 HgTe proposal, which directly enabled Molenkamp's experiment, and Fu, Moore and Balents on the three-dimensional theory, together with Hasan's 3D ARPES identification, cannot be represented in three names, and the citation must be worded so that it claims only the quantum spin Hall prediction, the Z2 classification and the first HgTe observation. The 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions is a legitimate point of caution, although I still read it as honouring a different step, phase transitions and quantum Hall precursors, and not time-reversal-protected edge and surface states and the Z2 classification. For my own earlier first choice, the case against waiting on B046 is that its key experiments are about eight years old, its pairing mechanism is unresolved, and its third slot (Bistritzer or Andrei, with Cao outside the credited names) has not been resolved by any argument in round 1.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B028 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, notes that the 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions and not the Z2 classification, and says B046 shares the allocation problem in sharper form and is more suited to a later year.
responses.response: I accept the core of this and it is the main reason I have moved. My round-1 reply to you was that B046 has the same prediction-then-experiment arc as B028, and that remains true. But you are right that B046 carries an unsettled pairing mechanism and an unresolved third slot, while B028 does not. I also agree that Hasan should enter only if the committee deliberately widens the citation to the 3D branch at the cost of a theory slot. I do not think the committee should do that, because the 3D theory credit would then be as incomplete as the 2D credit is now.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B046 first with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Andrei, argues Bistritzer's contribution is already represented in MacDonald's credit, and says a citation built on flat bands and correlated phases avoids resting the prize on the pairing mechanism.
responses.response: I agree that the citation can rest on flat bands and correlated phases, and I still hold that this is a real discovery. Your case for Andrei is also stronger than I allowed in round 1, since her STM and transport evidence of flat bands and van Hove singularities is independent of the 2018 experiments. That is exactly why I now see the allocation as unresolved: you and I credit the same two names plus different thirds, neither of us has an argument that excludes the other's choice, and Cao is absent from both. I cannot defend B046 as a first choice this year while the committee cannot settle who the third laureate is. Our disagreement on Bistritzer versus Andrei is therefore the reason I would move B046 to a later cycle, not a reason to press it now.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B034 first as a clean two-name invention-type discovery, says the clock is settled and independently reproduced, and notes the 2005 comb prize and the lack of a redefined second as the main caveats.
responses.response: I agree that B034 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and I keep it as my second alternative because of that. I still do not think clean attribution decides the case. I would put the question differently from how you do. Setting aside the redefinition of the second, which I agree should not drive the prize, the issue is whether lattice clocks opened a new physical regime or refined a technique the 2005 and 2012 prizes made possible. Your point that Ye's comb work overlaps with the 2005 prize also affects novelty for the credited pair. Your disclosure of the Hall-laboratory stay seems to me properly handled by transparency, as Lindroth and Pearce suggest, because the claim rests on the published record, and I would expect you to take part while the committee weighs it.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B034 first and calls the lattice clock a distinct scheme from the 2005 comb, with checkable, reproduced results, while she regards the 2016 prize overlap with B028 as more significant than Danielsson does.
responses.response: Your argument that the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate idea from the comb is persuasive and it weakens the novelty objection to B034. On the 2016 overlap, I think the distinction is physical and not only bibliographic: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz concerned topological order and phase transitions in the sense of quantized Hall conductance and the Haldane model, and Kane and Mele's contribution is a Z2 classification for time-reversal-invariant systems with a distinct prediction (helical edge states), which Molenkamp then observed. I accept that the committee may weigh the overlap differently. If it does, I would see B034, not B046, as the right fallback, because it is mature.

responses.point: Danielsson has moved from Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp for B028 and wants the citation worded so that the 2D result is not presented as the whole discovery.
responses.response: I welcome the move to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, which is also the trio I now propose, and I withdraw my opening support for Hasan on these grounds. I share your concern about citation scope, but I think the committee should accept it: with three names the citation can credit the quantum spin Hall prediction, the Z2 classification and the first observation, and it should not pretend to describe the whole field. I would not word it as a general prize for topological insulators, because that wording would imply a claim for the 3D branch that we cannot support with these names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat B028 as sufficiently separate from the 2016 topological-phases prize, and whether the citation can be worded to make that distinction explicit.
Whether leaving out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (and Hasan, Fu, Moore and Balents) misstates responsibility for the discovery. I rely on recalled priority history, not on documents in front of me.

Whether my move away from B046 is premature, since its maturity concern may ease within a few years and I regard it as a strong later-cycle candidate, but I cannot resolve the Bistritzer versus Andrei versus Cao allocation from the record supplied.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My field (electronic-structure theory and magnetism) is close to the physics of B028, B046 and B010, and I note that I ranked B046 first in round 1; I have no documented personal or institutional connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or any other credited name, and I do not claim one. I note Kroll's disclosed Hall-laboratory stay and Olsson's and Johansson's Chalmers link, and I regard both as matters for the committee to weigh in the open.
